text: REPEATABLE READ gives you everything READ COMMITTED gives you, plus one more guarantee: if you read a row once inside a transaction, reading that same row again inside the same transaction is guaranteed to return the same value.

The mechanism is simple. READ COMMITTED releases its shared lock the instant each statement's read finishes. REPEATABLE READ instead holds that shared lock until the whole transaction ends. That one difference is the entire gap between the two levels, and it's what closes the nonrepeatable-read problem from a couple lessons back.

But REPEATABLE READ only locks rows it has already read. A brand-new row, inserted after your first query ran, was never locked, because it didn't exist yet to lock. So phantom reads are still possible here -- the exact gap from the phantom-read lesson, unchanged.

The real cost of this guarantee is longer blocking. Other sessions trying to write to rows you've read now have to wait for as long as your whole transaction stays open, not just for one statement. That's more correctness bought with less concurrency -- the trade-off this whole cluster keeps coming back to.
So to recap: REPEATABLE READ prevents dirty reads and nonrepeatable reads, but still allows phantom reads, and it costs real concurrency to do it.
Next lesson, the strictest standard level of all: SERIALIZABLE, where phantom reads finally stop being possible too. See you there.
